title: DWS IQ Aegis
description:
DWS IQ Aegis

Sovereign Industrial Intelligence Platform for Dual-Use Manufacturing — part of the DWS IQ Industrial Intelligence suite

Product Overview

DWS IQ Aegis is the dual-use factory and critical-manufacturing layer of DWS IQ Industrial Intelligence — a standalone sovereign AI platform covering all 21 EU-regulated industries (including dual-use critical raw materials) for government agencies, military industry enterprises, and the dual-use manufacturing base that supplies Europe's defence sector. It optimizes and secures physical production facilities, not the tactical frontline. It packages sovereignty monitoring, orbital intelligence, agent governance, and EU AI Act compliance into a hardened platform — deployed on European cloud, enterprise private cloud, or customer-sited edge hardware, and never on a non-EU hyperscaler.

Named after Athena's shield — Aegis provides protection through intelligence, not just walls.

Product status: DWS IQ Aegis is in preorder. General availability September 2026. Pre-revenue. It is not described as "live" or "in production".

Aegis keeps critical compliance and control-room workflows running when the network cannot be trusted.

In a hybrid-war environment a manufacturing facility is dual-use critical infrastructure, and connectivity is an adversary-reachable dependency. For the control-room and critical / dual-use site deployment, local-first operation is an architectural requirement, not an option: loss of network connectivity must not stop production or the core compliance workflow. That deployment is scoped against five requirements — local execution and local evidence; local identity, logs and kill authority; no network dependency for the core outcome; cloud only for optional sync, backup or non-critical reporting; and graceful degradation specified in advance rather than discovered during an outage.

This is not a claim that every Aegis deployment is offline. EU-sovereign cloud remains a valid and fully supported mode for non-critical enterprise workloads, reporting and development. What is fixed is which mode the control-room use case requires.

This is a compliance requirement as much as a resilience one. The EU AI Act Article 12 record must exist for decisions taken during a disruption, not be reconstructed afterwards — an evidence chain that pauses when the uplink drops has a gap at exactly the moment the record matters most. NIS2 and the CER Directive impose the continuity obligation alongside it.

Locked decision, 30.07.2026 — see docs/field-notes/2026-07-30-network-independent-critical-operation.md. The tier boundary for delivering each of the five requirements is an open commercial decision (Q6 in that note); the premise above is product-wide.

Why Aegis exists: Defence and dual-use supply chains face the same EU compliance obligations as civilian ones (CSRD, CBAM, NIS2, CER Directive, CRM Act) — plus export control, data sovereignty, and dual-use regulation. No platform serves this intersection across all 21 industries with cross-vertical signal propagation. Aegis does.

Architecture — Two Layers, One Governed Loop

Aegis is a two-layer product. The layers solve different problems and are deliberately not served by one model.

| Layer | What it does | How it is served | Status | | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Physical — perception → action | Sees the facility and acts on it in real time: scene understanding, intent prediction, machine-vision oversight feeding the Control Room / Situation Room | An adopted open, on-device world model (NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge class) running on customer-sited edge hardware — not a model DWS pretrains | Planned — target 2026 Q4, gated on the on-device evaluation. title: DWS IQ Aegis Pilot (3 months)
description:
DWS IQ Aegis Pilot

Prove the local-first path before you buy the silicon — a 3-month scoped engagement, part of DWS IQ Aegis

What it is

A fixed-price, fixed-duration engagement that proves the complete local-first operational path for Aegis on infrastructure you already have — or on a compact edge appliance — before any DGX procurement.

The pilot exists because the control-room requirement is testable. In manufacturing control rooms, dual-use facilities and air-gapped plants, compliance execution cannot depend on external connectivity. That is either true of a deployment or it is not, and the way to find out is to run it and pull the cable — not to model it in a proposal.

What it proves

The five requirements that define a control-room deployment, demonstrated rather than asserted:

  1. Local execution and local evidence — the outcome is produced on site, and the evidence of it is written on site.
  2. Local identity, logs and kill authority — agent identity, the Article 12 record and the ability to stop an agent all resolve locally.
  3. No network dependency for the core outcome — the critical path completes with the uplink down.
  4. Cloud only for optional sync, backup or non-critical reporting — never the outcome, never the evidence chain, never the stop.
  5. Graceful degradation — specified in advance, then demonstrated, rather than discovered during an incident.

The acceptance KPI is binary and deliberately blunt. With the uplink severed for an agreed window: (i) does the piloted workflow run to completion, (ii) is the EU AI Act Article 12 record still being written locally, and (iii) can an operator still stop a running agent? All three must pass. A pilot that does not pass has produced a useful negative result — a valid outcome, not a defect — and you will have learned it for €19,990 instead of after a hardware programme.

What you get

  • A scoped architecture for your site, with the deployment mode named (Local / Edge, Hybrid, or EU-Sovereign Cloud) and justified.
  • A demonstrated uplink-down run against your own workflow.
  • The Article 12 evidence record, produced locally throughout the engagement.
  • Hardware sizing for production — informed by measured behaviour on your workload rather than a vendor spec sheet.
  • A written recommendation, including the honest one: if your workload does not need local-first, the pilot says so.

How the three months run

Five phases. The ordering is deliberate: the substrate is proven before the workflow exists, and the acceptance test is rehearsed before it is taken. Each phase has an exit gate, and a gate that does not pass is reported rather than worked around.

Phase 0 — Scoping and baseline · weeks 0–2 · no charge

Objective. Establish what "the core outcome" actually is, precisely enough that it can be tested.

  • We do: site, workflow and deployment-mode selection workshop; read-only audit of the source systems; criticality classification — every step in the workflow marked core (must survive an outage) or non-core; first draft of the degradation and reconciliation spec; baseline measurement of current-state behaviour.
  • You do: nominate the technical contact, the workflow owner, and the operator who will exercise kill authority; grant read-only access; agree the outage window, its date, and the isolation method.
  • Exit gate: a one-page signed scope — site, workflow, deployment mode, isolation method, and the three acceptance conditions written in your operational language, not ours.

On the isolation method. Continuously-operating sites cannot usually permit a physical cable pull, and a pilot that assumes one arrives at the acceptance test with no test. So the method is chosen in Phase 0 from a ranked ladder — physical disconnect, deny-all egress at the edge router, VLAN isolation of the Aegis segment, or host-level egress block — and recorded with what it does and does not demonstrate. Two rules make the choice safe: the block must be enforced above the stack (at your router, switch or hypervisor, administered by you — a system asked to disconnect itself has not been tested), and egress must be attempted and shown to fail before the run starts. The weaker methods prove less about the network boundary and exactly as much about the workload; the acceptance record names which was used, so a reader in three years knows what was demonstrated. - This phase fails if the workflow cannot be described as a terminating se
